newsitem.title: CHINA: China seen unaffected by soaring coffee prices.
newsitem.headline: China seen unaffected by soaring coffee prices.

text.p: Retail coffee prices in China will be mainly unaffected by a skyrocketing world market, with coffee sellers in fear of losing consumers for what is already seen as a pricey luxury item, analysts said on Friday.

New York arabica coffee futures shot up to their highest levels in two decades on Thursday in the third straight day of a rally that saw prices shatter the $3.00 a pound barrier and the July contract settle six percent up on the day at 314.18 cents.

Most mainland coffee retailers were unlikely to raise prices as a result of the rally to avoid alienating the nation's huge potential market, which coffee promoters are trying to woo away from their traditional tea, analysts said.
"Coffee is still a luxury and consumption is not high," one analyst said from Singapore. "They have to weigh against losing consumption."

Ground coffee in Beijing retails for 100 yuan ($12) a kg for a low-end blend containing domestic beans from Yunnan, while high-grade imported blend sells for more than 500 yuan. That compares with an average urban income of just 365 yuan a month in 1996.
"Looking at retail consumption levels, you'd just see a blip because the market is so small," said one analyst in Beijing who declined to be identified.

Although coffee giants Nestle and Starbucks have started battling for what is greedily being eyed as the next big market, China's 1.2 billion people drink only 20 grammes (0.7 ounces) of coffee per capita per year, industry figures show.
Wholesalers and retailers in Hong Kong, dismayed by the fresh rallies in prices, said on Friday they were considering price hikes.

Coffee stocks in producing and consuming countries are near 20-year lows and have spurred the five-month run-up in coffee futures, and the New York market has surged more than 175 percent since the beginning of the year.

But while multinational coffee firms were often protected by sophisticated financing and economies of scale, smaller firms trying to stay alive in China were being hit hard by the price rises, one Beijing wholesaler said.
"It's hurt us pretty bad," said Ron Thompson, vice-general manager of Arabica Coffee Roasters Co Ltd, which provides fresh roasted coffees to clients in several major Chinese cities.
Thompson said his firm, a small, private operation based in Beijing, would probably have to raise prices in the near future, putting it at a disadvantage with big multinationals such as Starbucks.
"They put in contracts when the price was low -- they're locked in already," said Thompson, who estimates his firm has about 10 percent of the Beijing market. "We're at the mercy of the market."
